title.title: Interoperability
title.subtitle: Why many chains need to talk — bridges, Cosmos IBC, Layer 0, and XRP

layer0Anim.headline: A tx travelling L2 → L1 → L0 → L1 → L2
steps: 1. L2 rollup posts a batch back to L1 (settlement)
2. L1 sends a cross-chain message through the Layer 0 hub
3. Layer 0 relays it to a different L1 (XCM / Warp / IBC)
4. Destination L1 delivers it down to its own L2

closed.heading: Blockchains are closed systems
closed.subtitle: Every chain runs on the internet, yet none can read, check or pay another. The isolation is built in.

cards.title: Its own validators
cards.desc: Each chain has its own group of computers that approves blocks. Bitcoin's miners never look at Ethereum, and Ethereum's validators never look at Bitcoin.

cards.title: Its own rules
cards.desc: Each chain has its own consensus rules for what counts as valid. A node accepts only what those rules let it check for itself.

cards.title: Its own ledger
cards.desc: A coin is just an entry in one chain's ledger (its state). A bitcoin exists only in Bitcoin's records, so there is nothing to physically send to Ethereum.

closed.whyLabel: Why it is built this way
closed.why: A blockchain is trusted because every node re-checks everything itself. Facts from another chain cannot be re-checked that way, so the chain ignores them — the same wall as the oracle problem.
closed.notEqualSub: Sharing the same cables is not sharing the same ledger.

svg.internet: The internet — every node of every chain is online

interop.heading: Why do blockchains need to talk to each other?
interop.subtitle: Closed systems are safe, but people, money and apps do not stay on one chain — so chains need a way to connect.
interop.recap: Bitcoin (Section 01) · Ethereum (Section 02) · Hyperledger Fabric (Section 03) — each one is its own island
interop.analogy: Imagine Gmail unable to send a message to Hotmail. Early email networks really worked like that: each service was closed until everyone adopted one shared standard (SMTP). Blockchains are mostly still at the "no shared standard" stage.

svg.caption: Each island validates only its own ledger. A coin cannot "swim" across.

islands.title: Three problems that follow
islands.intro: They appear as soon as value or users want to move between closed chains.

cards.title: Stranded assets
cards.desc: A bitcoin exists only on Bitcoin's ledger, so it cannot be used inside an Ethereum app. To get its value there, someone must hold the real coin and issue a stand-in on the other chain — and you now trust that someone.

cards.title: Costly connectors
cards.desc: Anything that links two chains has to hold, or vouch for, the value in transit. The connectors built to move value between chains have been crypto's costliest failures: about $2B stolen in 2022 alone.

cards.title: Split-up markets
cards.desc: Every chain has its own exchanges and pools. The same token can trade at one price on Ethereum and another on Arbitrum, and moving between them costs time and fees.

matters.solutionsLabel: Three ways to connect — compared next

solutions.label: Layer 0
solutions.sub: One security team for many chains

usecases.heading: Where this shows up in real life
usecases.subtitle: Six everyday situations, and how value crosses today.

items.title: Moving to a cheaper lane
items.scenario: You hold ETH on Ethereum, but a swap costs $20 in fees. You move it to Arbitrum or Base, where the same swap costs cents.

items.title: Using Bitcoin in DeFi
items.scenario: You want to earn yield on BTC inside an Ethereum lending app. A custodian holds the BTC and issues WBTC you can use.

items.title: One stablecoin, many chains
items.scenario: USDC lives natively on a dozen-plus chains; Circle's CCTP burns it on one chain and mints it on another. RLUSD settles on XRPL and Ethereum.

items.title: Game items that travel
items.scenario: A game runs on its own chain for speed (Ronin, Immutable), but players want to sell items on an Ethereum marketplace.

items.title: Private data, public settlement
items.scenario: A consortium keeps supplier data on a private Fabric network but wants final settlement or tokens on a public chain for liquidity.

items.title: Cross-border payment routes
items.scenario: A payment starts as a stablecoin on one chain and must arrive as a local-currency token on another — in one trip, not three hops.

interopCompare.heading: Three ways to connect chains
interopCompare.subtitle: Each one moves value or messages across chains; what changes is who you trust. Each gets its own section next.

ways.name: Bridges
ways.how: Lock the coin on one chain, issue a copy on the other.
ways.trust: An operator: a company or a few signers who hold the vault.
ways.analogy: A courier stores your luggage and hands you a claim ticket.

ways.name: IBC · protocol-native
ways.how: The two chains check each other's proofs directly.
ways.trust: The maths and the two chains themselves. No middleman.
ways.analogy: Two airports read each other's boarding passes.

ways.name: Layer 0
ways.how: Many chains sit under one shared validator set; messaging is built in.
ways.trust: The Layer 0's validators: one security team for every chain.
ways.analogy: One security team guards every terminal in the airport.

layer0.heading: Layer 0 — shared security beneath the L1s
layer0.leadB: to many L1s at once, so a cross-chain call is a
layer0.inOneLine: Like an internet backbone: many ISPs (L1s) plug into shared cables (L0) instead of each laying their own.

provides.title: Shared security
provides.desc: A pooled validator set secures every L1 connected to it. New chains inherit security on day 1.

provides.title: Native cross-chain messaging
provides.desc: L0 defines the message format and trust model (XCM, Warp) — no third-party bridge needed.

provides.title: Shared infrastructure
provides.desc: Block production, finality, governance and upgrades live at L0. L1s focus on application logic.

layer0.trust: The Layer 0's validators: the same set that finalises blocks also carries the messages.
layer0.risk: Everything inside is only as safe as the Layer 0 itself, and reaching a chain outside the club still needs a bridge.

layer02.heading: Layer 0: Known Platforms & Trade-offs
layer02.subtitle: Four networks usually called Layer 0, and the one choice that separates them: rent security or build your own.

platforms.name: Polkadot
platforms.tagline: Relay Chain validators secure every parachain; XCM is the built-in messaging.

platforms.name: Babylon
platforms.tagline: Bitcoin holders stake BTC to help secure other proof-of-stake chains — security borrowed from Bitcoin.

platforms.name: Avalanche
platforms.tagline: Primary Network plus sovereign Avalanche L1s (formerly subnets) with their own validators; Warp messaging between them.

platforms.name: Cosmos
platforms.tagline: Cosmos SDK chains (zones) with their own validators, linked by IBC; the Hub can lend security as an option.

models.title: Rent security
pros: Messaging between members is built in
models.con: Must follow the Layer 0's rules and pay it for security

models.title: Build your own
pros: Full control: own rules, fees and upgrades
models.con: Must recruit and pay its own validators

layer02.notL0: LayerZero is not a Layer 0: it is a messaging protocol between existing chains, closer to a bridge.

bridges.heading: What a bridge is — and how it works
bridges.subtitle: A bridge lets value from one chain be used on another. Nothing actually crosses: the original is locked on one side and a copy is issued on the other.
bridges.definition: A service that holds an asset on one chain and issues a matching "wrapped" copy on another, so the value can be used there.
bridges.analogy: A courier puts your luggage in storage and hands you a claim ticket. You travel with the ticket; the luggage never leaves. Hand the ticket back and you get the luggage.

steps.title: Lock
steps.desc: You send 1 ETH to the bridge's vault on Ethereum.

steps.title: Approve
steps.desc: The bridge operator sees the deposit and signs off on it.

steps.title: Mint
steps.desc: The bridge mints 1 wETH for you on Solana: your claim ticket.

steps.title: Burn to return
steps.desc: Burn the wETH on Solana and the operator releases your 1 ETH.

bridges.operatorBody: Someone you have to trust: one company (a custodian), or a multisig — a group of key-holders where, say, 5 of 9 must sign. The bridge is only as safe as they are.

flow.label: How a lock-and-mint bridge works
flow.back: Way back: burn the copy → the operator releases the original
flow.stays: the real coin never leaves Ethereum

hacks.name: Ronin Bridge
hacks.method: 5 of the 9 signer keys were stolen — enough to approve any withdrawal from the vault.

hacks.name: Wormhole Bridge
hacks.method: A signature check could be skipped — the attacker issued 120,000 wrapped ETH backed by nothing.

hacks.name: Nomad Bridge
hacks.method: A setup mistake made every message look valid. Hundreds of copycats emptied it within hours.

hacks.name: Harmony Horizon
hacks.method: Only 2 of 5 signers were needed — two stolen keys were enough.

bridgeRisk.heading: Bridges — useful, and the most hacked component in crypto
bridgeRisk.subB: was stolen from bridges in 2022 alone — about half of everything stolen in crypto that year.

vault.label: The honeypot: one vault backs every copy
vault.drained: Vault drained → every copy is a ticket to nothing
vault.caption: Every user adds to the same vault. The bigger it gets, the bigger the prize — that is the honeypot.

bridgeRisk.honest: Using a bridge is a trust decision, not a technical detail: you are trusting whoever controls the vault. Prefer a chain's official (canonical) bridge, and move only what you need.

dangers.title: One vault, everyone's coins
dangers.desc: The locked assets sit in a single contract. A bridge holding $500M is a $500M prize for whoever finds a bug.

dangers.title: A few people hold the keys
dangers.desc: Most bridges release funds when a small group of signers agree. Steal enough keys and the vault is yours.

dangers.title: Two chains, twice the complexity
dangers.desc: The bridge must understand both chains at once — different rules, timings and signature formats. More surface, more bugs.

safer.title: Chains verify each other (IBC)
safer.desc: No operator, no single vault — each chain checks the other's proofs. No known loss of funds from an IBC-protocol exploit so far.

safer.title: Official (canonical) bridges
safer.desc: Ethereum rollups' own bridges (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) are secured by the rollup's proof system, not by a separate group of signers.

safer.title: Rate limits & circuit breakers
safer.desc: Cap how much can leave per hour. Nomad was drained within hours — a limit would have saved most of it.

wrapped.heading: What a wrapped token is
wrapped.subtitle: The copy a bridge issues is a wrapped token. WBTC, wETH and friends are not the coin itself: they are a claim on a coin that someone else is holding.

svg.issuerPowers: can pause · can refuse to redeem
svg.caption: The wrapped balance is worth 1 BTC only while the custodian still holds 1 BTC and will hand it back.

cards.title: What it is
cards.desc: A token on one chain that stands for a coin held on another. 1 WBTC on Ethereum is a claim on 1 BTC kept by a custodian, much as a casino chip is a claim on cash at the cage.

cards.title: Who can redeem it
cards.desc: Usually not you. Only approved, identity-checked merchants swap WBTC back for BTC; everyone else sells it on an exchange. The price holds only while people believe the vault is full.

cards.title: Who can freeze it
cards.desc: The issuer. The WBTC contract can be paused by its owner, and a bridge operator can stop minting or releasing. If the vault is emptied, as at Wormhole in 2022, the copies are backed by nothing.

wrapped.noteLabel: Not every wrapper needs a custodian
wrapped.note: WETH on Ethereum itself is a plain contract: anyone swaps ETH for WETH and back 1:1 with nobody in the middle. The question to ask of any wrapped token is who holds the original.

bridgeHacks.heading: Why bridges get hacked — and the four largest hacks
bridgeHacks.subtitle: A bridge puts everyone's coins in one vault and lets a few keys open it. The four largest thefts, all in 2022, are the evidence.

points.title: One vault holds everyone's coins
points.desc: Every user's deposit lands in the same contract. The more people use the bridge, the bigger the prize.

points.title: A few signer keys control it
points.desc: Steal enough keys, or find one bug in the check, and the whole vault opens at once — not just one account.

svg.stolenNote: 5 of 9 is enough: the vault opens

bridgeHacks.evidenceLabel: The evidence — the four largest bridge hacks
bridgeHacks.takeaway: Prefer a chain's canonical/official bridge, move only what you need — and for any wrapped token, ask who holds the original.

cosmos.heading: Cosmos: The Internet of Blockchains
cosmos.subtitle: Sovereign chains connected by the IBC protocol, each built for one use case.
cosmos.archNote: Zones can also IBC each other directly (mesh)

properties.title: IBC Protocol
properties.desc: Inter-Blockchain Communication: each chain keeps a small copy of the other's block headers (a light client) and checks every proof itself, so messages and assets move without a middleman.

properties.title: Cosmos SDK
properties.desc: Go framework with ready-made modules (staking, governance, IBC) for building an app-specific chain. Used by Osmosis, dYdX v4, Celestia and 100+ chains.

properties.title: CometBFT (ex-Tendermint)
properties.desc: The consensus engine, formerly Tendermint: ~1-second blocks, instant finality, no forks. Each zone has a known validator set and stays secure while fewer than one-third are dishonest.

properties.title: App-Specific Sovereignty
properties.desc: Each chain sets its own fees, governance and upgrades, and does not compete for block space with other apps.

cosmos.beyondBodyB: (live 2025) extends IBC to Ethereum and other non-Cosmos chains without a centralised bridge.
cosmos.trust: The maths and the two chains' own validators, with no extra company or committee. A relayer only carries the message; it cannot forge it.
cosmos.risk: Only as strong as the weaker of the two chains, and both must speak IBC, which limits reach today.
cosmos.dydx: dYdX, a derivatives exchange, left its Ethereum rollup in 2023 for its own Cosmos chain: an app gets its own chain once it is big enough to justify one.

xrp.heading: XRP Ledger — a purpose-built settlement rail
xrp.subtitle: A public blockchain launched in 2012 to do one job well: move and exchange value. It is not a general smart-contract platform.
xrp.compareLabel: Two ways to design a chain

general.title: General-purpose platform
general.body: A blank computer. Every feature is a smart contract that someone wrote and deployed.
general.foot: Flexible — but every contract is new code that can have bugs.

rail.title: Purpose-built rail
rail.body: A fixed menu. The financial features are part of the protocol itself.
rail.foot: Limited menu — but fast, cheap and the same for everyone.

xrp.analogy: Ethereum is a kitchen: you can cook anything, and every dish is someone's own recipe. XRPL is a vending machine: a short fixed menu, served in seconds, the same way every time.

why.title: Payments and trading are built in
why.desc: An order-book exchange has been part of the protocol since 2012, and a native AMM since 2024. No contract to deploy or audit.

why.title: Fast and cheap by design
why.desc: A payment is final in 3–5 seconds and costs a fraction of a cent. The tiny fee is destroyed, which deters spam; there is no fee auction.

why.title: What you give up
why.desc: No general smart contracts on the main ledger. Richer logic runs on side networks such as the XRPL EVM sidechain (2025).

xrpHow.heading: How XRPL works — agreement by vote, not by mining
xrpHow.subtitle: No miners and no staking. A set of known validators votes on each batch of transactions, every few seconds.

svg.unl: Trusted validators (UNL: ~35 in the default list)
svg.caption: Each node listens to a list of validators it trusts. When 80% of them agree on the same set of transactions, the ledger closes — every 3–5 seconds. Below 80%, the network pauses rather than splits.

steps.title: Propose
steps.desc: Validators share the transactions they have seen.

steps.title: Vote
steps.desc: They compare and vote in rounds until they converge.

steps.title: Close
steps.desc: At 80% agreement the ledger is final. No rewards, no mining.

uses.title: Cross-border payments
uses.desc: XRP acts as a bridge currency: euros → XRP → pesos in seconds, without pre-funded bank accounts abroad.

uses.title: Stablecoins and tokenised assets
uses.desc: Issuers put tokens on the ledger, such as RLUSD, a New York-regulated dollar stablecoin (Dec 2024). You hold one by opening a Trust Line to its issuer.

uses.title: Institutional pilots
uses.desc: Central-bank digital currency pilots in Bhutan, Palau and Colombia run on XRPL technology (private versions).

uses.title: Reaching other chains
uses.desc: Through Axelar, XRPL apps send a payment and a message to 50+ chains in one call; Solidity apps run on the XRPL EVM sidechain.

xrpHow.honestBody: Anyone can run a validator, but most nodes use the default published list. You trust that list not to collude — a different bet from proof of work or proof of stake.

layers.heading: The Layers: L0 · L1 · L2
layers.subtitle: L2s stack on an L1; some L1s stand on a shared Layer 0.
layers.aria: Diagram of the layer stack. Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana are Layer 1 chains with no Layer 0 underneath; Lightning, Stacks and Rootstock sit on Bitcoin, and Arbitrum, Base and Optimism sit on Ethereum, settling their results on it; Solana has no L2 on top. A dashed strip notes that Bitcoin (through Babylon) and Ethereum (through EigenLayer restaking) also provide shared security to other chains. Moonbeam, Hydration and Bifrost stand on Polkadot, a shared Layer 0 that gives them security and messaging. Moving dots show transactions: slow on Bitcoin and Ethereum, fast on the L2s and Solana.

svg.restakers: ₿ Babylon: staked BTC  ·  Ξ EigenLayer: restaked ETH
svg.noL0Sub: Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana secure themselves, with their own miners and validators
svg.l0Sub: security and messaging for every chain plugged in

speed.title: Speed at each layer (not to scale)

quiz.question: You send 1 ETH through a lock-and-mint bridge and receive 1 wETH on another chain. A month later hackers empty the bridge's vault. What are you holding now?
options: 1 ETH — the bridge moved your coin across, so it is safe on the new chain.
1 wETH that the new chain's validators must replace, because they approved the mint.
1 wETH that is a claim on an empty vault — a ticket with nothing behind it.
Nothing at all — wrapped tokens are deleted automatically when a vault is drained.
quiz.explanation: A bridge never moves a coin. Your 1 ETH stayed in the vault on the first chain, and the wETH was only a claim ticket on it. Once the vault is empty the ticket is still in your wallet, but nothing backs it, so its price collapses — unless someone refills the vault, as Wormhole's backer did with $320M in 2022. That is why one shared vault guarded by a few keys makes bridges the biggest target in crypto, and why IBC and Layer 0 designs try to remove the middleman.

quiz2.question: Every Bitcoin node and every Ethereum node is connected to the same internet. Why can an Ethereum app still not simply use a bitcoin?
options: Each chain's nodes accept only what they can re-check under their own rules, and a bitcoin exists only as an entry in Bitcoin's ledger.
Bitcoin encrypts its ledger, so nobody outside the network can read it.
Regulators require each blockchain to be kept legally separate from the others.
It could, but Ethereum's validators charge a fee that makes it uneconomic.
quiz2.explanation: Being on the internet is not being interoperable. Each chain has its own validators, its own rules and its own ledger, and a blockchain is trusted because every node re-checks everything itself. Facts from another chain cannot be re-checked that way, so the chain ignores them — the same wall as the oracle problem. To use a bitcoin's value elsewhere, someone must hold the real coin and issue a stand-in.

quiz3.question: Two Cosmos chains exchange tokens over IBC. Who are you trusting?
options: A company that holds the tokens in a vault while they are in transit.
A committee of signers — say 5 of 9 — who approve each transfer.
The maths and the two chains' own validators: each chain checks the other's proofs itself, and a relayer only carries the message.
One shared validator set that secures both chains at once.
quiz3.explanation: Three routes, one question: who do you trust? A bridge: an operator, a company or a few signers. A Layer 0: one shared validator set. IBC: no middleman — each chain keeps a light client of the other and checks every proof itself. Its limits: it is only as strong as the weaker of the two chains, and both must speak IBC.

quiz4.question: The Ronin bridge was guarded by 9 signer keys. In 2022 attackers stole 5 of them and took $625 million. Why were 5 keys enough to take everything?
options: Each key unlocked one user's account, and those five accounts held most of the money.
With 5 keys the attackers could rewrite Ethereum's transaction history.
The keys let them create new ETH on Ethereum out of nothing.
The bridge released funds whenever 5 of the 9 signers approved, and every user's coins sat in the same vault.
quiz4.explanation: A bridge puts everyone's coins in one vault and lets a few keys open it. Five of nine signatures were enough to approve any withdrawal, so the whole vault opened at once — not just one account. That is why bridges are structurally risky, and why the advice is to prefer a chain's official (canonical) bridge and move only what you need.

quiz5.question: A team is launching a new chain. It wants to be secure from day one without recruiting its own validators. Which option fits, and what does it give up?
options: Launch as a fully sovereign chain: sovereign chains get their security for free.
Rent security from a Layer 0 (for example as a Polkadot parachain): secure from the start, but it must follow the Layer 0's rules and pay for that security.
Connect through LayerZero, the Layer 0 that lends its validators to new chains.
Open a lock-and-mint bridge to Ethereum: a bridge passes Ethereum's security on to the new chain.
quiz5.explanation: Shared security or full sovereignty: you rent one or build the other. Renting from a Layer 0 means inheriting its validators on day one, with messaging built in, in exchange for following its rules and paying it. A sovereign chain keeps full control but must recruit and pay its own validators. And despite the name, LayerZero is not a Layer 0: it is a messaging protocol, closer to a bridge.

quiz6.question: How does the XRP Ledger agree on which transactions are final?
options: Known validators vote: when 80% of the validators a node trusts agree, the ledger closes — every 3–5 seconds, with no mining and no staking.
Miners race to solve a puzzle, as on Bitcoin, only with much smaller blocks.
Validators lock up XRP as a stake and are drawn at random to propose blocks, as on Ethereum.
A single company server approves each payment and publishes the result.
quiz6.explanation: XRPL agrees by a vote among known validators: they propose, vote in rounds, and at 80% agreement the ledger is final — no rewards, no mining. Below 80% the network pauses rather than splits. The trade-off: most nodes use the default published list of validators, so you trust that list not to collude — a different bet from proof of work or proof of stake.

quiz7.question: Which line describes the division of labour between the layers correctly?
options: L0 adds cheap scale, L1 connects chains to each other, L2 secures and settles.
L2 secures and settles, L1 adds cheap scale on top of it, L0 stores the data.
L1 secures and settles, L2 adds cheap scale on top of it, L0 lets many chains share security and talk to each other.
L1 secures and settles, L0 adds cheap scale on top of it, L2 lets many chains share security.
quiz7.explanation: Layers are a division of labour. An L1 such as Bitcoin or Ethereum secures and settles. L2s — Lightning, rollups — stack on an L1 for speed and low fees and settle their results on it. A Layer 0 such as Polkadot sits underneath and gives the chains plugged into it shared security and messaging. Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana have no Layer 0 underneath: they secure themselves.

takeaways.title: Section 04 — Key Takeaways
items: Each chain is an island: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Fabric cannot read each other's ledgers — so value and messages need a route
Real needs drive it: cheaper L2 lanes, Bitcoin in DeFi, stablecoins on many chains, game assets, private data with public settlement
Three routes, one question — who do you trust? Bridges: an operator. IBC: the maths and both chains. Layer 0: one shared validator set
A bridge never moves a coin: it locks the original and issues a claim ticket. That one shared vault made bridges the most hacked component in crypto (Ronin $625M, Wormhole $320M)
XRP Ledger is a purpose-built payments rail: validators vote instead of mining, and it reaches other chains through Axelar rather than a bridge per pair
The stack in one line: L1 secures and settles, L2 adds cheap scale on top, L0 lets many chains share security and talk to each other

keyPoints.s4-closed: Every blockchain is a closed system: it checks only its own ledger. Being on the internet does not make chains interoperable.
keyPoints.s4-interop: People, money and apps do not stay on one chain, so closed chains need connecting — and every connection needs someone or something to trust.
keyPoints.s4-usecases: In every real case someone holds the asset or verifies the other chain; who that is, is the design question.
keyPoints.s4-ways: Three routes, one question: who do you trust — an operator, the two chains themselves, or one shared validator set?
keyPoints.s4-chooser: The safest connection is the one with the fewest people to trust.
keyPoints.s4-bridges: A bridge never moves a coin: a trusted operator locks the original on one chain and issues a claim ticket on the other.
keyPoints.s4-bridge-risk: Bridges are where the biggest thefts have happened; using one is a trust decision.
keyPoints.s4-wrapped: A wrapped token is an IOU; it is worth the original only while someone holds that coin and agrees to give it back.
keyPoints.s4-bridge-hacks: Every big bridge hack came down to a few stolen keys or one bug in the vault's checks; one shared vault turned it into a total loss.
keyPoints.s4-cosmos: Cosmos trades shared security for sovereignty; IBC lets chains verify each other without a middleman.
keyPoints.s4-layer0: A Layer 0 is a security team for hire; new chains inherit protection on day one.
keyPoints.s4-layer0-2: Shared security or full sovereignty: you rent one or build the other.
keyPoints.s4-xrp: XRPL is a payments rail, not an app platform; it is fast and cheap because it does less.
keyPoints.s4-xrp-how: XRPL agrees by a vote among known validators: final in seconds with no mining, at the price of trusting a published list.
keyPoints.s4-layers: Layers are a division of labour: L1 secures and settles, L2 scales on top of it, L0 lets many chains share security and talk.

chooser.heading: How should these two chains talk?
chooser.subtitle: Pick a situation, then a route, to see the fit and the main risk.
chooser.idle: Pick a situation on the left and a route in the middle…

scenarios.title: Move stablecoins to an L2
scenarios.desc: You hold USDC on Ethereum and want to use it on Arbitrum or Base, where fees are cents.

scenarios.title: One app, two chains, shared state
scenarios.desc: A lending app runs on two independent chains and needs balances and prices to stay in sync.

scenarios.title: Bank consortium meets a public chain
scenarios.desc: Banks run a private settlement chain but want tokens and final settlement on a public network.

bridge.label: Bridge
bridge.sub: Lock here, mint a copy there — an operator in the middle

ibc.label: IBC-style messaging
ibc.sub: Both chains verify each other's proofs directly

l0.label: Layer 0
l0.sub: Both chains sit under one shared validator set

bridge.text: Use the rollup's own (canonical) bridge. It is secured by the rollup's proof system, not by a separate group of signers.
bridge.risk: Going back to L1 is slow: hours on a ZK rollup, about 7 days on an optimistic one. 'Fast' third-party bridges fix that by adding an operator you must trust.

ibc.text: Ethereum and its rollups do not use IBC; the rollup already has a native, proof-secured route to L1.
ibc.risk: You would be building a second, less-tested path next to one that already exists.

l0.text: Arbitrum and Base are not parachains — there is no Layer 0 here. Ethereum itself is the shared security the rollups borrow.
l0.risk: Adding a Layer 0 means adding a validator set and a token you don't need for this job.

bridge.text: General message bridges (Axelar, LayerZero, Wormhole) can carry state updates between almost any two chains today — the widest reach.
bridge.risk: Your app's state now depends on the bridge's signer set. If it is compromised, both deployments can be corrupted at once — the honeypot problem.

ibc.text: If both chains speak IBC (Cosmos zones, or Ethereum via IBC Eureka), each verifies the other's proofs directly — messages travel without a middleman or a giant vault.
ibc.risk: Only as strong as the weaker chain, and both must implement the standard — reach is limited to the IBC ecosystem today.

l0.text: If both chains live inside the same Layer 0 (two parachains, two Avalanche L1s), messaging is native — XCM or Warp — and verified by the shared validators.
l0.risk: Only works inside the club. The moment one chain is outside, you are back to a bridge.

bridge.text: Anchor the private chain's state, or settle tokens, through a bridge the consortium controls. Simple and chain-agnostic — this is how most pilots start.
bridge.risk: The bridge operator is a single point of failure, and the regulator will ask who holds the keys. Governing that bridge becomes the real project.

ibc.text: A Fabric or Besu consortium chain does not speak IBC. You would have to rebuild it on an IBC-capable stack first — a migration, not an integration.
ibc.risk: A large rebuild for a standard the public chain you target may not support either.

l0.text: Run the consortium chain as a permissioned L1 inside a Layer 0 (an Avalanche L1 or a parachain). You keep your own validators and rules, yet messaging to the public network is native — the model JP Morgan piloted on Avalanche.
l0.risk: You are bound to that Layer 0's rules, token and validator security — and reaching chains outside it still needs a bridge.
